Do you call law enforcement now?","fact_ids":["sec11-F02","sec11-R02"]},"answer":{"text":"Yes. An immovable vehicle is one of the reasons to call at once.","fact_ids":["sec11-F02"]},"rationale":{"text":"Law enforcement hears immediately about injuries or deaths, immovable vehicles, fleeing drivers, and suspected intoxication.","fact_ids":["sec11-F02","sec11-R02"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec11-u01-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"After a crash","fact_ids":["sec11-F01","sec11-F02","sec11-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"What causes most crashes.","fact_ids":["sec11-F01","sec11-F02","sec11-F03"]},{"text":"What to exchange and report.","fact_ids":["sec11-F01","sec11-F02","sec11-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson opens the section on motor vehicle crashes. Most Texas crashes trace to speeding, botched yielding or stopping, and alcohol.","fact_ids":["sec11-F01","sec11-F02","sec11-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec11-u01-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Causes and information","fact_ids":["sec11-F01","sec11-R01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Speeding, yielding, stopping, alcohol.","fact_ids":["sec11-F01","sec11-R01"]},{"text":"Exchange names, plates, license, insurance.","fact_ids":["sec11-F01","sec11-R01"]},{"text":"Copy insurer and policy exactly.","fact_ids":["sec11-F01","sec11-R01"]}],"narration":{"text":"Most Texas crashes trace to speeding, botched yielding or stopping, and alcohol impairment. After a crash, drivers exchange names, addresses, phone numbers, vehicle numbers, plate numbers, license information, and insurance information when asked and when it is available. Copy the insurer's name and the policy number exactly as written. If there is a problem with an insurer, the insurance department hotline can help. Also note the crash location and how to contact any witnesses. So you leave a crash scene with the other driver's details, the insurance facts copied exactly, the place, and the witnesses.","fact_ids":["sec11-F01","sec11-R01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec11-u01-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"When to call or report","fact_ids":["sec11-F02","sec11-F03","sec11-R02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Call at once: injury or death.","fact_ids":["sec11-F02","sec11-F03","sec11-R02"]},{"text":"Immovable cars, fleeing drivers, intoxication.","fact_ids":["sec11-F02","sec11-F03","sec11-R02"]},{"text":"Minor crashes: written report in ten days.","fact_ids":["sec11-F02","sec11-F03","sec11-R02"]}],"narration":{"text":"Law enforcement must hear immediately about any crash with an injury or death, a vehicle that cannot be moved, a driver who flees, or a driver suspected of intoxication. For crashes that police do not investigate, with no injury or death and less than one thousand dollars of property damage, a written report goes to the transportation department on its form within ten days of the crash. So there are two paths: an immediate call for the serious situations, and a written report within ten days for the minor ones that no officer investigates at the scene.","fact_ids":["sec11-F02","sec11-F03","sec11-R02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec11-u01-s4","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Call now or report later","fact_ids":["sec11-R02","sec11-F02","sec11-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Four reasons to call at once.","fact_ids":["sec11-R02","sec11-F02","sec11-F03"]},{"text":"Minor uninvestigated: ten-day report.","fact_ids":["sec11-R02","sec11-F02","sec11-F03"]},{"text":"Under one thousand dollars, no injury.","fact_ids":["sec11-R02","sec11-F02","sec11-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a trap built from the reporting rules. Learners sometimes think every crash needs an immediate police call, or that a written report covers any crash at all. Neither is right. Call law enforcement at once for an injury or death, an immovable vehicle, a fleeing driver, or suspected intoxication. A written report within ten days is for crashes that police do not investigate, with no injury or death and less than one thousand dollars of property damage. When a question describes a crash, check for the four call triggers first; if none applies and police did not investigate, think ten days.","fact_ids":["sec11-R02","sec11-F02","sec11-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec11-u01-s5","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the immovable car","fact_ids":["sec11-F02","sec11-R02","sec11-F01"]},"lines":[{"text":"The other car cannot move.","fact_ids":["sec11-F02","sec11-R02","sec11-F01"]},{"text":"Call now?","fact_ids":["sec11-F02","sec11-R02","sec11-F01"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: after a crash, the other car cannot be moved from the road. Do you call law enforcement now? Work out your answer before reading on. Yes. An immovable vehicle is one of the four reasons to call immediately, along with an injury or death, a driver who flees, and suspected intoxication. While you wait, exchange names, addresses, phone numbers, plate numbers, license details, and insurance details, copying the insurer's name and policy number exactly, and note the location and any witnesses. Four triggers call for an immediate call.","fact_ids":["sec11-F02","sec11-R02","sec11-F01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec11-u01-s6","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Crash reporting in brief","fact_ids":["sec11-F01","sec11-R01","sec11-F02","sec11-F03","sec11-R02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Top causes: speed, yielding, alcohol.","fact_ids":["sec11-F01","sec11-R01","sec11-F02","sec11-F03","sec11-R02"]},{"text":"Exchange details; copy insurance exactly.","fact_ids":["sec11-F01","sec11-R01","sec11-F02","sec11-F03","sec11-R02"]},{"text":"Call now or report in ten days.","fact_ids":["sec11-F01","sec11-R01","sec11-F02","sec11-F03","sec11-R02"]}],"narration":{"text":"Let us sum up. Most Texas crashes trace to speeding, botched yielding or stopping, and alcohol impairment. After a crash, exchange names, addresses, phones, vehicle numbers, plates, license facts, and insurance facts when asked and available, copying insurer names and policy numbers exactly, and note the location and witness contacts. Tell law enforcement immediately about injuries or deaths, immovable vehicles, fleeing drivers, and suspected intoxication. Crashes that police do not investigate, with no injury or death and under one thousand dollars of damage, need a written report within ten days. Next, stopping duties.","fact_ids":["sec11-F01","sec11-R01","sec11-F02","sec11-F03","sec11-R02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec11-u02","module_id":"sec11-m02","objective_ids":["sec11-u02"],"title":{"text":"Stopping duties and fleeing penalties","fact_ids":["sec11-F04","sec11-F06","sec11-R03"]},"why_how":[{"text":"The law requires drivers to stop after a crash and give their information, and it punishes fleeing.","fact_ids":["sec11-F04","sec11-F06"]},{"text":"Penalties for fleeing climb with the harm the crash caused.","fact_ids":["sec11-F05","sec11-F07","sec11-R04"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"On a highway, Lee's car is lightly damaged in a crash with another car, and both cars can still be driven.","fact_ids":["sec11-F06","sec11-R03"]},"reasoning":{"text":"Vehicle-damage-only crashes demand an immediate stop near the scene and a prompt move of drivable cars to a frontage road, cross street, or suitable spot.","fact_ids":["sec11-F06","sec11-R03"]},"result":{"text":"Lee stops, both drivers move their cars to a cross street, and they exchange names, addresses, registration, and insurers.","fact_ids":["sec11-F06"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking you must leave drivable cars in the lane until police arrive after a minor crash.","fact_ids":["sec11-F06","sec11-R03"]},"correction":{"text":"When main-lane cars stay drivable after a vehicle-only crash, you move them promptly to a suitable spot.","fact_ids":["sec11-R03","sec11-F06"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Stop, identify, aid or move.","fact_ids":["sec11-R03"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"Fleeing a crash causes two hundred fifty dollars of damage to the other car. What class of offense is that?","fact_ids":["sec11-F07","sec11-R05"]},"answer":{"text":"Class B.","fact_ids":["sec11-F07"]},"rationale":{"text":"Property-only fleeing is Class C below two hundred dollars and Class B with jail at two hundred dollars or more.","fact_ids":["sec11-R05","sec11-F07"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec11-u02-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Stopping and staying","fact_ids":["sec11-F04","sec11-F06","sec11-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Duties after injury crashes.","fact_ids":["sec11-F04","sec11-F06","sec11-F05"]},{"text":"Duties after vehicle-only crashes.","fact_ids":["sec11-F04","sec11-F06","sec11-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson covers what the law requires after a crash, and what happens to drivers who flee. The duties depend on the kind of crash. After a crash with an injury or death, you stop, stay, identify yourself, and render aid. After a crash that only damages vehicles, you stop, move drivable cars clear of the main lanes, and identify yourself. We will then look at the penalties for fleeing, which climb with the harm the crash caused, from death and serious injury down to property damage, with a split at two hundred dollars for property-only crashes.","fact_ids":["sec11-F04","sec11-F06","sec11-F05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec11-u02-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"After an injury or death crash","fact_ids":["sec11-F04","sec11-R03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Stop at or near the scene.","fact_ids":["sec11-F04","sec11-R03"]},{"text":"Give name, address, registration, insurer.","fact_ids":["sec11-F04","sec11-R03"]},{"text":"Render reasonable aid.","fact_ids":["sec11-F04","sec11-R03"]}],"narration":{"text":"After a crash with an injury or death, stop immediately at or near the scene without blocking traffic more than needed, return at once if you passed it, and stay. Give your name, address, vehicle registration, and insurer to the injured people and to those attending the vehicles, and show your license when asked and available. Render reasonable aid, including taking an injured person to a doctor or hospital when it is needed or requested. So the duties are to stop, return, stay, identify yourself, show your license on request, and help the people who were hurt.","fact_ids":["sec11-F04","sec11-R03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec11-u02-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"After a vehicle-only crash","fact_ids":["sec11-F06","sec11-R03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Stop at or near the scene.","fact_ids":["sec11-F06","sec11-R03"]},{"text":"Move drivable cars clear.","fact_ids":["sec11-F06","sec11-R03"]},{"text":"Give the same information.","fact_ids":["sec11-F06","sec11-R03"]}],"narration":{"text":"After a crash that damages only vehicles that were being driven or attended, stop immediately at or near the scene. If the cars in the main lanes can still be driven, move them promptly to an investigation site, a frontage road, a cross street, or another suitable spot. Return at once if you passed the scene, and stay. Give the same information as in an injury crash: your name, address, registration, and insurer, and show your license on request. So the vehicle-only duties match the injury-crash duties, except that rendering aid is replaced by moving drivable cars clear.","fact_ids":["sec11-F06","sec11-R03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec11-u02-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Penalties for fleeing","fact_ids":["sec11-F05","sec11-R04","sec11-F07","sec11-R05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Death: second-degree felony.","fact_ids":["sec11-F05","sec11-R04","sec11-F07","sec11-R05"]},{"text":"Serious injury: third-degree felony.","fact_ids":["sec11-F05","sec11-R04","sec11-F07","sec11-R05"]},{"text":"Property: Class C below two hundred.","fact_ids":["sec11-F05","sec11-R04","sec11-F07","sec11-R05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Fleeing a crash with a death is a second-degree felony, with a fine up to ten thousand dollars and two to twenty years in the Texas prison system. Fleeing a crash with serious bodily injury is a third-degree felony, with a fine up to ten thousand dollars and two to ten years. Fleeing a crash with plain injury brings up to five years in prison or one year in county jail, and a fine up to five thousand dollars. Fleeing a vehicle-damage crash is Class C, up to five hundred dollars, under two hundred dollars of damage, or Class B with jail at two hundred or more.","fact_ids":["sec11-F05","sec11-R04","sec11-F07","sec11-R05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":43,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec11-u02-s5","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"The property split","fact_ids":["sec11-F07","sec11-R05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Under two hundred dollars: Class C.","fact_ids":["sec11-F07","sec11-R05"]},{"text":"Two hundred or more: Class B.","fact_ids":["sec11-F07","sec11-R05"]},{"text":"Class B adds jail.","fact_ids":["sec11-F07","sec11-R05"]}],"narration":{"text":"For crashes that only damage property, the fleeing penalty splits at two hundred dollars of damage. Below two hundred dollars, fleeing is a Class C offense with a fine up to five hundred dollars. At two hundred dollars or more, it is a Class B offense with a fine up to two thousand dollars and up to one hundred eighty days in jail. The same Class C and Class B ladder applies to fleeing after striking an unattended vehicle or a fixture. So for any property-only crash, the amount of damage, above or below two hundred dollars, decides the class of the offense.","fact_ids":["sec11-F07","sec11-R05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec11-u02-s6","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Death, serious injury, injury","fact_ids":["sec11-R04","sec11-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Death: second-degree felony.","fact_ids":["sec11-R04","sec11-F05"]},{"text":"Serious injury: third-degree felony.","fact_ids":["sec11-R04","sec11-F05"]},{"text":"Plain injury: prison or jail and fine.","fact_ids":["sec11-R04","sec11-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a trap built from the fleeing ladder. The penalties for fleeing an injury crash depend on how badly someone was hurt. A death makes it a second-degree felony, with two to twenty years. Serious bodily injury makes it a third-degree felony, with two to ten years. Plain injury brings up to five years in prison or one year in county jail, and a fine up to five thousand dollars. Learners often swap the two felony levels. When a question names the harm, match it to its step: death goes with second-degree, serious injury with third-degree.","fact_ids":["sec11-R04","sec11-F05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec11-u02-s7","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the property split","fact_ids":["sec11-F07","sec11-R05","sec11-F06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Fled; two hundred fifty dollars damage.","fact_ids":["sec11-F07","sec11-R05","sec11-F06"]},{"text":"What class?","fact_ids":["sec11-F07","sec11-R05","sec11-F06"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: a driver flees a crash that caused two hundred fifty dollars of damage to the other car, and no one was hurt. What class of offense is that? Work out your answer before reading on. It is Class B, because the damage is two hundred dollars or more. Class B brings a fine up to two thousand dollars and up to one hundred eighty days in jail. Had the damage been under two hundred dollars, it would have been Class C with a fine up to five hundred dollars. Either way, the driver was required to stop, stay, and give information.","fact_ids":["sec11-F07","sec11-R05","sec11-F06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec11-u02-s8","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Stopping duties in brief","fact_ids":["sec11-F04","sec11-F06","sec11-R03","sec11-F05","sec11-R04","sec11-F07","sec11-R05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Injury crash: stop, identify, aid.","fact_ids":["sec11-F04","sec11-F06","sec11-R03","sec11-F05","sec11-R04","sec11-F07","sec11-R05"]},{"text":"Vehicle-only: stop, move clear, identify.","fact_ids":["sec11-F04","sec11-F06","sec11-R03","sec11-F05","sec11-R04","sec11-F07","sec11-R05"]},{"text":"Fleeing penalties climb with harm.","fact_ids":["sec11-F04","sec11-F06","sec11-R03","sec11-F05","sec11-R04","sec11-F07","sec11-R05"]}],"narration":{"text":"To wrap up, after an injury or death crash, stop at or near the scene, return and stay, give your name, address, registration, and insurer, show your license on request, and render reasonable aid. After a vehicle-only crash, stop, move drivable main-lane cars to a suitable spot, and give the same information. Fleeing a death crash is a second-degree felony, serious injury a third-degree felony, and plain injury up to five years in prison or a year in jail. Fleeing a property-only crash is Class C under two hundred dollars of damage and Class B with jail at two hundred or more. Next, property strikes.","fact_ids":["sec11-F04","sec11-F06","sec11-R03","sec11-F05","sec11-R04","sec11-F07","sec11-R05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec11-u03","module_id":"sec11-m03","objective_ids":["sec11-u03"],"title":{"text":"Property strikes and helping","fact_ids":["sec11-F08","sec11-F09","sec11-R06"]},"why_how":[{"text":"When you hit an unattended car or a fixture, the law still requires you to find the owner or leave notice.","fact_ids":["sec11-F08","sec11-F09"]},{"text":"Hit-and-run victims report crashes because uninsured motorist coverage pays reported cases.","fact_ids":["sec11-F10","sec11-R07"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Pia scrapes a parked car in an empty lot and cannot find the owner.","fact_ids":["sec11-F08","sec11-R06"]},"reasoning":{"text":"Unattended-vehicle strikes demand an owner search or a visible written notice carrying names, addresses, and crash circumstances.","fact_ids":["sec11-F08","sec11-R06"]},"result":{"text":"Pia leaves a visible note with her name, address, and what happened.","fact_ids":["sec11-F08"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking you should quickly move an injured person to a more comfortable spot.","fact_ids":["sec11-F10"]},"correction":{"text":"Helpers avoid moving victims, and preserve their positions if a move is essential, while summoning skilled aid.","fact_ids":["sec11-F10","sec11-R07"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Find the owner or leave a note.","fact_ids":["sec11-F08","sec11-R06"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"You stop to help at a crash and an injured driver says they are fine. What should you do?","fact_ids":["sec11-F10","sec11-R07"]},"answer":{"text":"Summon skilled help anyway.","fact_ids":["sec11-F10"]},"rationale":{"text":"Helpers summon skilled aid without trusting denials of injury, avoid moving victims, stanch bleeding, and shelter them.","fact_ids":["sec11-F10","sec11-R07"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec11-u03-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Property and people","fact_ids":["sec11-F08","sec11-F09","sec11-F10"]},"lines":[{"text":"Unattended cars and fixtures.","fact_ids":["sec11-F08","sec11-F09","sec11-F10"]},{"text":"Hit-and-runs and first aid.","fact_ids":["sec11-F08","sec11-F09","sec11-F10"]}],"narration":{"text":"This final lesson in the section covers crashes where no other driver is present, and what to do for people who are hurt. If you strike a parked, unattended vehicle, or a fixture such as a fence, landscaping, or a structure, the law still sets out duties for you. We will cover those duties and the penalties for leaving. Then we turn to hit-and-run victims and why they should report, and to the steps for helping an injured person at a crash: stating the location clearly, summoning skilled help, keeping the victim still, stopping bleeding, and giving shelter.","fact_ids":["sec11-F08","sec11-F09","sec11-F10"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec11-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Unattended cars and fixtures","fact_ids":["sec11-F08","sec11-F09","sec11-R06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Unattended car: owner or visible note.","fact_ids":["sec11-F08","sec11-F09","sec11-R06"]},{"text":"Fixture: owner search and notice.","fact_ids":["sec11-F08","sec11-F09","sec11-R06"]},{"text":"Same Class C and Class B ladder.","fact_ids":["sec11-F08","sec11-F09","sec11-R06"]}],"narration":{"text":"If you strike an unattended vehicle, stop immediately and search for the owner to give your name and address, or leave a visible written notice with your name, your address, and the circumstances of the crash. If you strike a fixture, landscaping, or a structure, make a reasonable search for the owner, give notice of the crash with your name, address, and registration, and show your license on request. An uninvestigated crash under one thousand dollars to any one person, with no injury or death, needs a written report within ten days. Leaving falls under the same Class C and Class B ladder.","fact_ids":["sec11-F08","sec11-F09","sec11-R06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec11-u03-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Hit-and-runs and first aid","fact_ids":["sec11-F10","sec11-R07"]},"lines":[{"text":"Victims report for coverage.","fact_ids":["sec11-F10","sec11-R07"]},{"text":"State the location; call skilled help.","fact_ids":["sec11-F10","sec11-R07"]},{"text":"Do not move victims; stop bleeding.","fact_ids":["sec11-F10","sec11-R07"]}],"narration":{"text":"If you are the victim of a hit-and-run, report the crash for investigation, because uninsured motorist coverage pays reported cases. If you stop to help an injured person, state the location clearly when you call, and summon skilled help even if the person says they are not hurt. Avoid moving the victim; if a move is essential, preserve their position. Stop serious bleeding with a clean, thick pad pressed on the wound, and shelter the victim from heat or cold. So help means calling with a clear location, keeping the person still, controlling bleeding, and giving shelter.","fact_ids":["sec11-F10","sec11-R07"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec11-u03-s4","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Note for cars, notice for fixtures","fact_ids":["sec11-R06","sec11-F08","sec11-F09"]},"lines":[{"text":"Unattended car: owner or visible note.","fact_ids":["sec11-R06","sec11-F08","sec11-F09"]},{"text":"Fixture: owner search, notice, registration.","fact_ids":["sec11-R06","sec11-F08","sec11-F09"]},{"text":"Possible ten-day report for fixtures.","fact_ids":["sec11-R06","sec11-F08","sec11-F09"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a trap built from two property rules. After hitting an unattended car, you search for the owner or leave a visible written note with your name, address, and what happened. After hitting a fixture, landscaping, or a structure, you make a reasonable search for the owner and give notice with your name, address, and registration, and a ten-day written report may be needed for an uninvestigated crash under one thousand dollars to any one person. Learners sometimes think no duty applies when no one is around. Both rules apply, and leaving brings the same Class C or Class B penalty.","fact_ids":["sec11-R06","sec11-F08","sec11-F09"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec11-u03-s5","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the injured driver","fact_ids":["sec11-F10","sec11-R07"]},"lines":[{"text":"Injured driver says they are fine.","fact_ids":["sec11-F10","sec11-R07"]},{"text":"What do you do?","fact_ids":["sec11-F10","sec11-R07"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: you stop to help at a crash, and an injured driver says they are fine. What should you do? Work out your answer before reading on. Summon skilled help anyway. The handbook says not to trust denials of injury.
